Mention them only in the executive summary at the front of the package
Record status in the plans and POA&M and add the residual risk to the register
why: Partial implementation is recorded openly, with the weakness, milestones and residual risk, so that the authorizing official can decide knowingly. Overstating, deleting or burying the facts misleads the decision.

q: The team built a different logging mechanism than the one in the approved plan. What should happen before the assessment?
opts: Document the change and update the security and privacy plans
Keep the old plan so that it can be compared with the new mechanism
Tell the assessor in person and leave the written plan unchanged
Delete the logging section so that no one can say it differs
why: Changes to the planned implementation are documented and the plans are updated so assessors test what exists. Leaving the plan stale or removing the section makes the control unassessable.

q: A small organization adopts a 300-page policy set copied from a large firm. Staff do not follow most of it. What is the best improvement?
opts: Add many more pages so that every possible situation is covered in detail
Document proportionately so policies describe what is really done
Keep the policies and train staff to say that they always follow them closely
Archive the policies and rely on verbal instructions from team leaders instead
why: Documentation should fit the organization's purpose, scope and risk profile and describe real practice. More pages, rehearsed answers or verbal instructions do not close the gap between paper and practice.

q: Which statement about the classic management, operational and technical control types is most accurate for the current NIST catalog?
opts: Rev. 5 no longer uses those classes, but the terms remain in common use
SP 800-53 Rev. 5 still groups every control into exactly those three classes
The classes were replaced entirely by the Low, Moderate and High baselines
The classes apply only to privacy controls and never to security controls
why: Rev. 5 organizes controls by family and no longer uses the three classes, although SP 800-18, older material and the outline still use the terms. The baselines and privacy controls are separate ideas.

q: Which three belong in a control implementation strategy? (Choose three.)
opts: The assessor's final findings
The authorization decision for the system
Resources and funding needed
How effectiveness will be judged
A timeline with milestones and dependencies
why: A strategy covers resources, schedule and measures of effectiveness. The authorization decision and final findings come after implementation and assessment.

q: Which two are examples of technical controls in the classic NIST grouping? (Choose two.)
opts: Visitor escort procedures at a data center
Annual security awareness training
Audit logging of user activity
A risk assessment policy
Multifactor authentication
why: Logging and multifactor authentication are carried out by system mechanisms. Training and escort procedures are operational, and the policy is a management control.

q: Which two statements about the first control in an SP 800-53 family (the policy and procedures control) are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It applies only to systems categorized High
It calls for a designated official to manage the policy and procedures
It replaces the need for any other control in the family
It requires review and update at a defined frequency and after defined events
why: Each family opens with policy and procedures, a responsible official and a review cycle. It does not replace the other controls, and it is not limited to high systems.

q: A risk register and a POA&M are the same document with two names.
opts: True
False
why: The register records risks and decisions, while the POA&M tracks remediation of weaknesses with resources, milestones and dates. They are linked but different.

q: Individual training records are retained so that the organization can show who was trained and when.
opts: True
False
why: Training is documented and records are kept for a defined period as audit evidence.

q: A compensating control must provide comparable protection to the control it replaces and be justified and approved.
opts: True
False
why: Without comparable protection and approval, the substitution is just an unmet requirement.

q: Controls can be implemented in any order because dependencies matter only during assessment.
opts: True
False
why: Dependencies matter during implementation; building a control before its prerequisites can make it unusable or untestable.

q: Common controls describe a type of control in the same way that technical and operational do.
opts: True
False
why: Common describes who implements a control (once, for many systems). Technical, operational and management describe the nature of the control.

q: An assessor is about to start testing a production system. Which document should be agreed and approved first?
opts: The security assessment report from the last cycle
The plan of action and milestones
The authorization decision letter
The security assessment plan with rules of engagement
why: The plan defines scope, methods, schedule and rules, and must be approved before testing so everyone agrees what will happen. The POA&M and SAR are created from results, and an authorization decision comes after assessment.

q: An assessor wants to confirm that a firewall rule set matches what the SSP says. Which assessment method most directly checks actual behavior of the mechanism?
opts: Examine the SSP only
Interview
Review of the organization's policy
Test
why: Testing exercises the mechanism and compares actual behavior to expected behavior. Interviews reveal what people say, and reading the SSP or policy shows intent, not what the device actually does.

q: An assessor reviews an access control policy and finds it well written. Staff say they follow it, but nobody has checked the accounts. What is the best next step?
opts: Mark the control other than satisfied because policies cannot be evidence
Skip the control because it is administrative
Mark the control satisfied because the policy and staff statements agree
Examine or test the real account configurations
why: Documents and interviews show intent and perception; operation needs evidence from the system. Marking it satisfied is premature, marking it failed without checking is unfair, and administrative controls are still assessed.

q: During an assessment, the system owner fixes a misconfiguration the assessor found, and the assessor retests it successfully. How should the report reflect this?
opts: Remove the finding from the report because it was already fixed
Convert the fixed finding into a formally accepted risk
Record the finding along with the remediation and retest
Leave the finding open until the next scheduled assessment occurs
why: The report is a record of what was found and what was done. Deleting it hides history, leaving it open ignores the retest, and risk acceptance is not needed for a resolved weakness.

q: An AO wants stronger confidence for a high-impact system. Which assessment choice best increases credibility of the results?
opts: Reduce the number of controls assessed to save time
Use assessors independent of the developers and operators
Have the ISSO assess the controls they personally implemented and operate
Rely only on self-attestation signed by the system owner
why: Independence reduces bias and increases trust, particularly for higher-impact systems. Self-assessment and attestation lack independence, and fewer controls reduce coverage.

q: A tester wants to run an exploit against a payment server during business hours. The rules of engagement do not mention the server. What should the tester do?
opts: Stop and obtain written approval before proceeding
Proceed because the system is generally in scope for the program
Run it on a similar test system and report the result as production
Proceed with the test but notify the owner afterward
why: Testing must stay within the agreed rules, and changes need approval. Proceeding without it risks disruption and legal exposure, notice afterward is too late, and misreporting test results is dishonest.

q: A vulnerability scan reports hundreds of critical findings. Several are in software that the system does not use. What is the best action?
opts: Accept the risk of all of them without review
Validate findings and remove false positives
Report all of them because the tool rated them critical
Ignore all scan findings because scanners are unreliable
why: Scan results require validation to separate real weaknesses from false positives. Blind reporting wastes effort, ignoring findings leaves true weaknesses, and accepting risk requires analysis.

q: An assessment finds weaknesses that cannot be fixed before the planned authorization date. What should the organization create to track the fixes?
opts: A new security categorization
A new risk management strategy
A plan of action and milestones
A revised system boundary
why: The POA&M lists the weaknesses, resources, owners, milestones and dates. The strategy and categorization are not changed by findings, and changing the boundary to hide weaknesses is improper.

q: A cloud provider hosts a federal system and is assessed against FedRAMP requirements. Which party performs the independent assessment?
opts: The software vendor's sales engineer
The cloud provider's development team
A third-party assessment organization
The agency's help desk
why: The 3PAO provides independent assessment for FedRAMP. The provider's own team lacks independence, and the others are not assessors.

q: A customer wants evidence that a service provider's controls operated effectively across the previous nine months. Which report is most appropriate?
opts: A SOC 2 Type I report
A vendor-written security whitepaper
A SOC 2 Type II report
A list of the provider's policies
why: Type II tests operating effectiveness over a period. Type I covers design at a point in time, and whitepapers and policy lists do not provide independent evidence of operation.

q: The assessor documents that a backup control was implemented but the restores were never tested, so the desired outcome was never confirmed. Which aspect of control effectiveness is missing?
opts: Categorization of the system
Independence of the assessor
Producing the desired outcome
Implementation of the control at all
why: Effectiveness means correct implementation, operation as intended and producing the desired outcome. Backups exist, so implementation is present; untested restores leave the outcome unproven. The other options are unrelated to the gap.

q: A privacy officer asks whether the assessment will cover whether PII is used only for stated purposes. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: Only encryption of the PII is within the scope for this assessment step
Privacy is assessed only by external privacy auditors, never by the team
Privacy is outside the scope of the RMF assessment step entirely
Privacy controls are assessed with security controls, including PII use
why: Privacy controls are assessed together with security controls, including purpose limitation and notice. Limiting scope to encryption misses PT-type controls, and privacy is part of the RMF.

q: Which two methods are standard assessment methods in SP 800-53A? (Choose two.)
opts: Presume
Interview
Examine
Delegate
Estimate
why: Examine, interview and test are the three methods. Estimate, presume and delegate are not assessment methods.

q: Which three items are normally included in a security assessment plan? (Choose three.)
opts: The controls and objectives to be assessed
Rules of engagement and schedule
The methods and objects to be used
The AO's final authorization decision
The final list of weaknesses found
why: The plan defines what, how and when before testing. The decision and findings come afterward.

q: Which two statements about the POA&M are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It is created before any testing occurs
It replaces the security assessment report
It is updated until each item is closed
It grants permission to leave weaknesses unfixed indefinitely
It lists weaknesses with responsible parties, milestones and completion dates
why: The POA&M tracks remediation commitments and is updated as items close. It does not excuse neglect, it complements the SAR, and it is created from findings after testing.

q: An assessor decides whether the residual risk is acceptable.
opts: True
False
why: The assessor reports findings; the authorizing official decides whether the risk is acceptable.

q: The assessment plan should be approved before testing begins.
opts: True
False
why: Approval ensures agreement about scope and rules, preventing unauthorized or disruptive testing.

q: Interviewing staff is sufficient evidence that a technical control is operating.
opts: True
False
why: Interviews show what people believe; technical controls need examination or testing.

q: A SOC 2 Type I report tests operating effectiveness over a period.
opts: True
False
why: Type I covers design at a point in time. Type II tests operation over a period.

q: A penetration test and a vulnerability scan provide the same kind of evidence.
opts: True
False
why: A scan lists possible weaknesses; a penetration test shows whether they can be exploited and what follows.

q: Assessment results for inherited controls can be reused when they are current and relevant.
opts: True
False
why: Reuse reduces effort, but stale results do not give valid assurance.

q: An assessor is asked to begin testing next week, but the objectives, systems in scope and schedule are only described verbally. What should happen first?
opts: Document objectives, scope, schedule and deliverables and get agreement
Begin testing the systems the assessor thinks are most important first
Start with the vulnerability scan and refine the scope as findings arrive
Wait until the authorizing official reads the final report before scoping
why: The preparation task is to outline objectives, scope, resources, schedule, deliverables and logistics and finalize the plan with the stakeholders. Starting testing without agreed scope risks coverage gaps, and a final report cannot exist before testing.

q: A high-impact system has few assessors and a short deadline. How should the team decide how much depth and coverage to apply to each control?
opts: Give more depth and breadth to higher-risk controls and systems
Apply the same depth and breadth to every control to appear fair
Apply maximum depth to controls that are easy to test
Apply the least depth to controls that were hard to implement
why: Level of effort follows risk and the decision being supported, so high-risk controls get more depth and coverage. Uniform effort wastes resources, testing ease is not a risk measure, and hard-to-implement controls deserve more scrutiny, not less.

q: A new assessor wants to reuse last year's penetration test as evidence. The system has since changed its architecture and added an interconnection. What is the best judgment?
opts: Accept it in full because any prior test remains valid for two years
Reject all earlier documents and begin the assessment from nothing at all
Accept it if the same vendor performed both of the penetration tests
Use it as background only; the changes mean current testing is needed
why: Prior results can inform planning, but stale results do not give valid assurance when the system has changed. Rejecting every earlier document wastes useful context, and the vendor does not make the evidence current.

q: The assessment plan has been drafted and the team is eager to start. What must happen before testing begins?
opts: The system owner signs the security assessment report in advance
The AO or a designated approver reviews and approves the plan
The plan of action and milestones is closed out for all items
The ISSO approves the plan and also performs the testing
why: Approval of the plan establishes the expectations, level of effort and rules before testing. The report and POA&M come later, and having the ISSO both approve and test undermines independence.

q: An assessor wants to know whether disabled accounts can still sign in to a critical application. Which technique answers this most directly?
opts: A vulnerability scan of the application and its web server
Reading the account management policy aloud together with the system owner
Control testing: attempt to sign in with accounts that are disabled
A review of the vendor's marketing description of the product
why: Control testing exercises the specific mechanism and compares actual behavior to the expected result. A scan looks for known weaknesses broadly, and reading policy or marketing shows intent, not behavior.

q: An assessor needs to know whether several scanner-reported weaknesses can actually be exploited and chained to reach sensitive data. Which technique fits best?
opts: A second run of the same vulnerability scan, repeated later
A review of the firewall rule set and the router settings
Penetration testing under agreed rules of engagement
An interview with the network administrator and a manager
why: Penetration testing validates exploitability and chains weaknesses as an attacker would. A repeated scan adds no new kind of evidence, and a rule review or interview shows configuration and belief, not the result of an attack.

q: An assessor has a configuration export showing that logging is enabled, but wants stronger evidence that logs are actually produced and reviewed. What is the best way to validate it?
opts: Accept the configuration export because configuration is the evidence
Corroborate it with log samples and records of the reviews
Ask the system owner to confirm in writing that logging works
Delete the control from the plan because it cannot be verified
why: Evidence is validated by corroborating it with an independent source such as logs and review records. A single export or a written assurance from the owner is weak, and removing the control hides the gap.

q: The assessor delivers an initial report that lists risks, mitigation summaries and preliminary findings. Why is it issued before the final report?
opts: So the system owner can confirm accuracy and begin corrective action
So the authorizing official can issue the decision before final results
So the findings can be removed from the report if the owner objects
So the report can be published to customers before the owner sees it
why: The initial report gives stakeholders the chance to check facts and start remediation, and the final report reflects the outcome. It does not let the AO decide early, findings are not deleted at the owner's request, and the owner sees it first.

q: Management disagrees with a preliminary finding and asks that it be deleted. The evidence supports the finding. What is the best response?
opts: Delete the finding in order to preserve the working relationship with management
Keep the finding, record management's disagreement and let the AO weigh both
Downgrade the finding without any new evidence just to settle the dispute
Add the finding only to a private note kept by the lead assessor
why: Findings reflect evidence, and disagreements are recorded so decision makers can weigh them. Deleting, downgrading without evidence or hiding a finding undermines the independence and value of the assessment.

q: For a finding, the stakeholders agree to buy insurance for the financial loss and to keep the activity running. Which risk response is mainly being chosen?
opts: Transfer or share
Avoid
Accept without any further action
Mitigate by adding technical controls
why: Insurance moves part of the financial impact to another party, which is sharing or transferring risk. Avoidance would end the activity, acceptance would take no action, and mitigation would add controls.

q: The system owner says a misconfiguration was fixed after the initial report. What should the assessor do before changing the finding's status?
opts: Accept the owner's statement as sufficient proof and close the finding
Leave the finding open until the next annual assessment is performed
Close it only if the same person who made the fix signs it off
Reassess the control to confirm the fix works and adds no weakness
why: Corrective actions are reassessed and validated before closure. Accepting a statement is not validation, and waiting a year or letting the fixer certify the fix are not appropriate either.

q: In the final report a control that the assessor never tested is listed as not applicable. What is wrong with this?
opts: Nothing; any control that was not tested can be called not applicable
Untested controls must always be reported as compliant to avoid delay
Not applicable needs a documented reason; untested is a coverage gap
Untested controls must be removed from the control baseline for the system
why: A control is not applicable only when there is a recorded reason, such as a missing capability. Controls that were simply not tested are a gap in coverage that must be explained, not hidden under another label.

q: The assessor writes that the organization "should adopt stronger monitoring" with no link to any finding. What is the best improvement to the recommendation?
opts: Tie each recommendation to a finding, with priority and rationale
Make the recommendation mandatory and assign it to the assessor
Remove all recommendations so that the report states only the facts found
Replace it with a list of commercial products to buy
why: Recommendations should be linked to findings, prioritized and explained, and remain advice for the owner. Making them the assessor's task, removing them or listing products does not help decision makers.

q: After the assessment, a team lists twelve deficiencies and asks which to address first. Which approach is best?
opts: Fix them in exactly the order in which they appear in the report
Fix the easiest first and leave the rest for the next cycle
Rank by risk, asset value and exposure, and consider quick wins
Fix first the items that are named in the oldest policy document
why: Prioritization follows risk, asset value, exploitability and regulatory exposure, with attention to cheap fixes. Order of appearance, ease alone or policy age are not risk-based.

q: A POA&M item shows a completion date six weeks out, but it depends on a vendor patch with no release date and a change window that does not yet exist. What is the main weakness?
opts: The date ignores dependencies, resources and the time needed to mitigate
The item should be removed from the POA&M because vendors control patches
The date is fine because POA&M dates are never reviewed by anyone later
The item must be reclassified as an accepted risk immediately by the owner
why: A risk response plan estimates resources and time including dependencies. A date that ignores them will slip. Removing the item or reclassifying it as accepted does not address the risk.

q: A customer audits a supplier against the customer's own security requirements. What kind of audit is this?
opts: A first-party audit
A third-party certification audit
A second-party audit
A self-assessment questionnaire
why: A second-party audit is done by a customer or partner on a supplier. A first-party audit is internal, and a third-party audit is by an independent body such as a certification body.

q: During an ISO/IEC 27001 certification audit, the auditor finds that a required internal audit program has never been run at all. How is this most likely classified?
opts: An observation that needs no response or follow-up from the organization
A minor nonconformity that the auditor corrects personally
A compliant result because other controls were operating
A major nonconformity that can block certification until corrected
why: A required part of the management system that is missing entirely is a systemic failure and is usually a major nonconformity, which must be corrected and verified. Observations and minor items describe lesser issues, and auditors do not fix findings.

q: Which three belong in the preparation for an assessment or audit? (Choose three.)
opts: Establishing stakeholder roles and responsibilities
Outlining objectives, scope, schedule and deliverables
Issuing the final authorization decision
Reviewing previous assessments and system documentation
Closing all POA&M items
why: Preparation sets roles, scope, schedule and deliverables and reviews existing evidence. The authorization decision and POA&M closure come after testing and reporting.

q: Which two statements about the final assessment report are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It is approved by the assessor alone with no review for accuracy
It omits findings that management has already agreed to fix
It states each result as compliant, non-compliant or not applicable with reasons
It records recommendations tied to findings and any disagreement from management
why: The final report records results, justified not-applicable decisions, recommendations and disagreements. It does not hide fixed findings, and it is reviewed with the system owner for factual accuracy.

q: Which two items does a risk response plan normally contain? (Choose two.)
opts: A promise to accept every risk without review
Resources and time required to mitigate each risk
The assessor's personal opinion of the system owner
Prioritized residual risks and deficiencies with owners
why: The plan turns findings into commitments with priorities, owners, resources and time. Opinions of individuals and blanket acceptance are not part of it.

q: Which three are SP 800-115 technique groups for security testing and assessment? (Choose three.)
opts: Target vulnerability validation
Target identification and analysis
Review techniques
Authorization decision techniques
Contract negotiation techniques
why: SP 800-115 groups techniques into review, target identification and analysis, and target vulnerability validation. The other two are not groups in that guide.

q: Corrective actions for non-compliant findings are reassessed and validated before the finding is closed.
opts: True
False
why: Reassessment confirms the fix works and introduces no new weakness; otherwise the closure is only a claim.

q: A control that was not tested in an assessment can be reported as not applicable without any explanation.
opts: True
False
why: Not applicable needs a documented reason. An untested control is a coverage gap to be explained.

q: A second-party audit is performed by a customer or partner on its supplier.
opts: True
False
why: Second-party audits sit between internal (first-party) audits and independent third-party audits.

q: A finding of other than satisfied can mean the assessor could not obtain enough information to decide.
opts: True
False
why: SP 800-53A says other than satisfied covers anomalies in implementation or operation and also cases where evidence is insufficient, with the reasons given in the report.

q: Assessment recommendations are binding orders that the assessor can enforce.
opts: True
False
why: Recommendations advise the system owner and authorizing official, who decide the response.

q: Which set of documents is typically provided to the authorizing official as part of the authorization package?
opts: Raw scanner output and the related email threads
The organization's annual budget and staffing plan for security
Only the system's architecture and data flow diagram
Plans, assessment reports, the POA&M and an executive summary
why: The package supports a risk decision with plans, results, remediation commitments and summary. Budgets, raw data and diagrams alone do not inform acceptance of risk.

q: The AO reviews a package showing several moderate weaknesses, with a credible POA&M and compensating monitoring in place. Risk is within tolerance. Which decision is most appropriate?
opts: Delegate the decision to the assessor
Issue an authorization to operate with conditions
Issue a denial because any weakness blocks authorization outright
Delay the decision until every weakness is fully closed
why: An AO may authorize operation at acceptable risk and attach conditions. Denial for any weakness is not risk-based, indefinite delay is not required, and the decision cannot move to the assessor.

q: An assessment reveals a severe unpatched weakness in a system that handles sensitive data, with no plan or compensating control, and the residual risk is far above tolerance. What should the AO do?
opts: Issue a denial of authorization to operate
Remove the weakness from the report
Authorize anyway because of the schedule
Ask the ISSO to accept the risk instead
why: When risk is unacceptable the AO denies authorization. Schedule pressure is not a valid reason, the ISSO does not hold risk acceptance authority, and altering the report is dishonest.

q: An agency wants to use a cloud service that another agency has already authorized and has the full package available. Which decision type is most appropriate?
opts: Common control authorization
Denial of authorization to operate
Authorization to use
A new full authorization to operate with no reuse
why: Authorization to use lets an agency rely on another organization's package and make its own decision. Denial does not apply, common control authorization approves controls provided to many systems, and a full new ATO ignores reuse.

q: A shared data center's physical controls are being relied upon by a dozen systems. What decision approves those controls so systems can inherit them?
opts: Denial of authorization to operate
Interim system disposal
Authorization to use
Common control authorization
why: Common control authorization approves the shared controls separately from individual systems. ATU is for a system or service used by another agency, and the others do not fit.

q: An authorization expires today and the system owner asks to continue operating because there have been no incidents. What is the correct response?
opts: The assessor can approve continued operation until the next assessment cycle begins
The ISSO can extend the termination date informally in the plan document
It lacks a current authorization; the AO must renew it or adopt ongoing authorization
No action is needed if there were no security incidents during the period
why: Authorization lasts until its termination date unless the AO renews it or ongoing authorization is in place. Lack of incidents is not a decision, and neither the ISSO nor assessor can extend it.

q: An organization wants to stop periodic reauthorization and let the AO decide continuously. Which prerequisite is essential?
opts: An additional external certification of the whole organization
The removal of the POA&M process from the program
A mature continuous monitoring program
A higher impact level for every system in the portfolio
why: Ongoing authorization depends on reliable, current information from monitoring. Raising impact, adding certifications or removing the POA&M does not supply it.

q: A CIO asks whether passing a compliance audit means the organization is secure. What is the best answer?
opts: Yes, because compliance with a standard guarantees security for the organization
Yes, provided the audit was performed by a respected third party firm
No, because audits never reflect how real controls behave in practice
Not necessarily; compliance shows requirements were met, not risk reduced
why: Meeting requirements is not identical to managing risk; checklists can miss real threats. Audits do reflect controls, and a third party does not turn compliance into security.

q: A federal agency plans to use personal identifiers to retrieve records about individuals. Which compliance artifact is publicly published to describe such a records system?
opts: An interconnection security agreement
A plan of action and milestones
A business impact analysis
A system of records notice
why: The Privacy Act requires agencies to publish a SORN. The others are internal security and continuity documents.

q: A company operates under a contract clause and a national privacy law that conflict on data retention. Which approach is best?
opts: Map both and apply the stricter requirement with legal advice
Follow the contract only, since the company signed it
Follow whichever of the two is cheaper to implement
Ignore the law because it is less specific than the contract
why: Mapping exposes the conflict and the stricter requirement usually governs, with legal advice. Ignoring law or choosing by cost creates liability.

q: The authorizing official includes a condition requiring that two high-priority POA&M items close within 90 days. At day 120, one is still open. What is the best response?
opts: Extend the date silently without telling the AO
Treat it as a failed condition and revisit the decision
Reclassify the finding as low so that it can be closed
Ignore it because conditions of authorization are advisory only
why: Conditions are enforceable and unmet conditions may lead to modification or revocation of the authorization. Treating them as advisory, extending silently or relabeling findings undermines the decision.

q: Which two statements about authorization to operate are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It can be inherited automatically by any agency
It may carry conditions and a termination date
It guarantees the system is free of weaknesses
It is issued by the system owner
It states that the AO accepts the risk of operating the system
why: An ATO is a risk acceptance decision with possible conditions and dates. It does not guarantee absence of weaknesses, the AO issues it, and other agencies must decide for themselves.

q: Which three are valid outcomes or decision types in the RMF Authorize step? (Choose three.)
opts: Automatic approval by the assessor
Approval by the ISSO alone
Authorization to operate
Authorization to use
Denial of authorization to operate
why: The AO may authorize operation, deny it, or authorize use of another organization's authorized system; assessors and ISSOs do not decide.

q: Which two actions are appropriate when an AO sees incomplete or outdated documents in the package? (Choose two.)
opts: Approve and hope the details are correct
Remove the documents from the package
Treat the uncertainty as part of the risk analysis
Request updated documents before deciding
why: Decisions should rest on accurate information, so the AO asks for updates and factors in uncertainty. Approving blindly or removing documents weakens decision quality.

q: FedRAMP is based on NIST SP 800-53 baselines.
opts: True
False
why: FedRAMP baselines are drawn from SP 800-53 with cloud-specific additions.

q: A denial of authorization to operate means the process failed.
opts: True
False
why: A denial is a legitimate, risk-based outcome; the system can be resubmitted after fixes.

q: The AO issues the authorization decision.
opts: True
False
why: The AO has the authority and accountability for accepting risk and issuing the decision.

q: Ongoing authorization is possible without any continuous monitoring program.
opts: True
False
why: It relies on current information from monitoring to support continuing risk acceptance.

q: The SSP lists twelve components in the boundary, but the assessment report covers only nine. What should happen before the package goes to the authorizing official?
opts: Delete three components from the SSP so that the documents agree
Submit as is and let the AO decide whether the difference matters
Ask the assessor to rename the nine components so the count matches
Reconcile the documents and assess or explain the three components
why: The package must be consistent, and untested components are a coverage gap that must be assessed or explained. Deleting components hides them, and renaming does not change what was tested. Submitting the mismatch pushes the problem to the decision maker.

q: A federal system owner has finished and reviewed the authorization package for a new system. To whom is it submitted for the authorization decision?
opts: The authorizing official or a designated representative
The security control assessor who performed the assessment
The ISSO who wrote the system security plan
The vendor that supplied the system software
why: The package supports the authorizing official's risk decision. The assessor already produced the assessment, the ISSO helped write the plan, and the vendor has no authority over the decision.

q: Two authorizing officials in the same agency accept very different open weaknesses on similar systems. What would most directly make future decisions consistent?
opts: A rule that each AO must write a longer explanation after deciding
Documented acceptance criteria from the risk strategy, set in advance
A shared mailbox where the AOs can talk about their decisions afterward
A requirement that assessors also vote on every decision
why: Criteria set in advance, such as limits on severity and age of open items, give officials a common basis. Longer explanations and discussion after the fact do not change the standard, and assessors do not decide risk.

q: The assessment shows ten moderate weaknesses, all on the same internet-facing subsystem and chainable into one attack path. How should the authorizing official judge the risk?
opts: Consider the combined effect of the weaknesses, not each one alone
Treat the overall risk as moderate because every single item is moderate
Ignore the weaknesses because none is rated high
Treat each as independent and accept them one by one
why: Aggregate residual risk considers weaknesses that combine or share a path, which can exceed the rating of any single item. Judging items alone understates risk.

q: An authorizing official plans to accept a risk that, if realized, would also affect a partner agency connected to the system. What is the best practice?
opts: Accept the risk without telling the partner so that no delays arise
Inform the partner's owner and get concurrence before accepting
Ask the partner to accept the risk on the official's behalf
Ask the assessor to make the decision for both agencies
why: Risk treatment that affects other organizations needs their awareness and agreement, while the accountable official still decides. Hiding it, shifting the decision or asking an assessor are all inappropriate.

q: An authorizing official says in a meeting that the remaining risk is acceptable but nothing is written down. What should the team do?
opts: Treat the spoken statement as sufficient and file the meeting notes
Record the statement in the risk register only and skip the decision letter
Have it recorded in writing with rationale, conditions, owner and date
Wait for the next assessment to decide whether it was accepted
why: Acceptance must be documented formally, signed by an authorized official, with rationale and conditions. Informal notes or leaving it open do not create a record anyone can rely on.

q: After an authorization decision, which parties should receive formal notification in addition to the system owner?
opts: Only the security control assessor, who needs the decision to file the final report
Only the vendor, so that it can update its product roadmap and release plans
Common control providers, inheriting system owners and risk oversight officials
No one, because the decision is an internal matter for the AO to keep private
why: Decisions and significant risks are communicated to the people who depend on the system or oversee risk. Limiting notification to the assessor or vendor, or to no one, leaves those parties unaware of the conditions.

q: In an ISO/IEC 27001 program, who issues the certificate once the audit is complete?
opts: ISO itself, after reviewing the audit report
The organization's top management, by self-declaration
The certification body, after it reviews the audit results
The auditing team's lead auditor alone, with no further review
why: Certification bodies, accredited to do so, make the certification decision and issue the certificate. ISO writes the standard and does not certify, and self-declaration is not certification.

q: A merchant has completed its PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire. What does it normally provide to its acquirer to show compliance?
opts: A SOC 2 Type II report from its hosting provider for the same period
An ISO/IEC 27001 Statement of Applicability for the whole company
An authorization to operate issued by its own department manager
An attestation of compliance supported by the questionnaire
why: PCI DSS compliance is shown with an attestation of compliance backed by the questionnaire or an assessor's report. A SOC 2 report, a Statement of Applicability and an internal ATO are different instruments.

q: A contractor completes a CMMC Level 2 self-assessment. Where must the results and affirmation be submitted?
opts: To the card brands through the merchant's acquiring bank
To the supervisory authority within seventy-two hours of the assessment
To the HHS Office for Civil Rights through its public breach portal
Into the Department of Defense's Supplier Performance Risk System
why: CMMC results and affirmations are recorded in the DoD systems, including SPRS. Card brands, GDPR supervisory authorities and the HHS Office for Civil Rights belong to PCI DSS, GDPR and HIPAA.

q: A sales brochure says the company's entire platform is authorized, but only one module completed the authorization. What is the best response?
opts: Leave it, since the remaining modules will probably be authorized
Add a footnote in small print and keep the headline unchanged
Remove the authorized module from the brochure instead
Correct the statement to match the authorized scope and status
why: External statements must reflect the real scope and status; overstating compliance creates legal and trust risk. A footnote or hoping for later approval does not fix a misleading claim.

q: Which three checks belong in the review of an authorization package before submission? (Choose three.)
opts: Evidence for inherited controls is attached and current
The documents are written in the same font and layout
The package has no executive summary
The boundary and components match across the documents
POA&M items trace back to assessment findings
why: Consistency of the boundary, traceability of the POA&M and current evidence for inherited controls make the package reliable. Formatting is cosmetic and an executive summary is part of the package.

q: Which two items belong in the formal notification of an authorization decision? (Choose two.)
opts: The private notes of the assessor about the system owner
The names of employees who failed security training
The decision type and any conditions
The effective date and the termination date or ongoing authorization status
A promise that the system has no remaining weaknesses
why: The notice states the decision, conditions and dates. Personal notes, a guarantee of no weaknesses and unrelated staff information do not belong.

q: Which two statements about residual risk documentation are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It is recorded only in the assessor's private notes
It is recorded in writing with rationale, conditions and the accepting official
It is kept in the authorization decision, POA&M and risk register
It is unnecessary when every weakness has a compensating control
why: Formal documentation names the accepting official and the rationale and is kept in the records leaders and assessors use. Compensating controls reduce risk but residual risk is still recorded.

q: Several low-rated weaknesses can combine into a risk that is higher than any single item suggests.
opts: True
False
why: Aggregate risk considers shared attack paths and dependencies, so the combined effect can exceed the individual ratings.

q: When stakeholders concur with a risk treatment, they take over the authorizing official's accountability for it.
opts: True
False
why: Concurrence shows agreement and awareness, but the accountable official still decides and remains responsible.

q: A SOC 2 report is issued by the service organization about its own controls.
opts: True
False
why: The report is an opinion written by an independent CPA firm; the service organization supplies a description and assertion.

q: An authorization decision should be communicated in a formal written notice that states conditions and dates.
opts: True
False
why: The signed notice is the record of the decision and its terms.

q: Acceptance criteria for risk are best defined after the authorizing official has made the decision.
opts: True
False
why: Criteria set in advance give consistent decisions; criteria invented afterward only justify what was already decided.

q: A system owner wants to add a new interconnection to a partner network. What should happen before the change is implemented?
opts: An immediate update of the authorization termination date
Implementation first, then analysis only if problems appear
An impact analysis, followed by change approval
Deletion of the SSP so that it matches reality again
why: Impact analysis before change shows how risk is affected and whether reassessment is needed. Analysis after the fact is reactive, changing a date is not an analysis, and deleting the plan removes needed documentation.

q: Which sequence best reflects the SP 800-137 ISCM process?
opts: Buy tools, deploy sensors, review reports, then define the strategy
Define strategy, establish, implement, analyze, respond, review
Report, respond, define, implement, establish, then review the program
Assess every year, authorize every year, then archive the results
why: The process starts with strategy and loops through review and update. Tools before strategy lack direction, and other orders are illogical or describe a periodic model.

q: A monitoring team wants to set assessment frequency for each control. Which factor should be considered?
opts: Volatility, system impact, threats and risk tolerance
The alphabetical order of the control identifiers
Only the schedule preferred by the tool vendor
One identical frequency for every control
why: ISCM frequency is risk-based, so higher volatility, impact and threat lead to more frequent monitoring. Alphabetical order and uniform schedules ignore risk, and vendor preference alone is not a risk factor.

q: A team migrates a system from one cloud provider to another. Which characterization is most appropriate?
opts: A change that affects only the documentation and plans
A significant change that may need reassessment
A routine change that needs no further review at all
A change the ISSO may declare insignificant without analysis
why: A new hosting environment affects many controls and risks. Treating it as routine or documentation-only ignores impact, and skipping analysis undermines the judgment.

q: The same configuration drift keeps appearing after each patch cycle, undoing a hardened setting. What is the best response?
opts: Ignore it because patches routinely change settings anyway
Find the root cause, fix the process and add drift detection
Disable the hardening requirement that keeps being undone
Accept the risk indefinitely without any further review
why: Repeated drift signals a process flaw that automation and baseline control can fix. Ignoring it or dropping the requirement weakens the system, and indefinite acceptance requires analysis and AO approval.

q: A system is being retired. Which action is part of proper disposal?
opts: Format the drives and then record the media as sanitized
Keep it connected to the network for the convenience of users
Shut the system down and leave the data in place for later use
Sanitize media by sensitivity, update inventory and remove connections
why: Disposal includes handling data, inventory and connections. Leaving data or relying on formatting risks exposure, and leaving connections active leaves a path to the organization.

q: The AO asks for monthly posture reports. The security team sends the raw output of five scanners. What is the best improvement?
opts: Summarize it into prioritized risk information for the AO
Send even more raw scanner output to the AO every week
Reduce reporting to once a year to save the team time
Send only the good news and omit the rest of the results
why: Reports should be understandable and decision-oriented. More raw data adds noise, less frequent reporting weakens oversight, and filtering bad news is dishonest.

q: An incident reveals that a critical patch was applied after eight weeks. Which monitoring improvement is most relevant?
opts: Eliminate vulnerability scanning to reduce the noise
Patch everything at once without any testing
Track patch latency and prioritize by severity
Move patching to an annual maintenance schedule
why: A metric for patch latency with risk-based prioritization improves timeliness. Removing scanning, unsafe mass patching and annual schedules would worsen risk.

q: A company outsources payroll processing. Which approach best provides ongoing oversight of the provider?
opts: Trust the provider's marketing claims and website
Assume the provider's responsibility ends the company's accountability
Contract rights to audit and incident notice, plus assurance reports
An annual questionnaire completed by the provider alone
why: Oversight works when contract terms and evidence allow real verification. A questionnaire is thin, marketing is not evidence, and accountability for the data stays with the company.

q: A contingency plan has never been exercised. Which action best addresses the weakness?
opts: Archive the plan so it is safely stored
Declare the plan effective simply because it exists
Exercise the plan, record results and update it
Rewrite the plan with many more pages of detail
why: Exercises show whether the plan works and expose gaps. More pages without testing, archiving or declaring it effective leave the assumption untested.

q: Which two items should be updated after significant changes or reassessment? (Choose two.)
opts: The organization's mission statement
The POA&M
The ISC2 code of ethics
The security and privacy plans
The vendor's marketing material
why: Plans and the POA&M must reflect the current state. The others are unrelated to authorization information.

q: Which two activities are typical parts of continuous monitoring? (Choose two.)
opts: Ending monitoring after authorization
Ongoing assessment of selected controls at defined frequencies
Reporting the security and privacy posture to decision makers
Assessing every control every day
why: Monitoring is risk-based and continuing, with reporting. Assessing everything daily is unrealistic, and ending monitoring defeats its purpose.

q: A security impact analysis should be performed before a change is made.
opts: True
False
why: It informs approval and whether reassessment is needed.

q: Formatting a drive satisfies media sanitization for sensitive data.
opts: True
False
why: SP 800-88 requires methods like clear, purge or destroy suited to sensitivity; formatting is generally not enough.

q: The final task of the Monitor step is system disposal.
opts: True
False
why: Disposal closes the life cycle, including data handling and inventory updates.

q: Every control must be assessed with the same frequency in continuous monitoring.
opts: True
False
why: Frequency depends on factors such as volatility, impact and threat.

q: A team proposes upgrading a database engine. The upgrade replaces the cryptographic module with one that has not been validated, and a compliance requirement calls for validated cryptography. What is the best action?
opts: Approve it because the new module offers noticeably better performance
Approve it and then update the compliance requirement afterward to match
Approve it because database engine upgrades are always routine changes
Analyze risk and compliance impact and do not approve it as proposed
why: Change analysis weighs risk, operational effect and compliance requirements. A change that breaks a mandatory requirement is not approved as proposed. Performance and routine labels do not change the requirement.

q: A developer pushes a configuration change straight to production and files a ticket the next morning. What is the most accurate description?
opts: A normal change, since the ticket was eventually created the next day
An unauthorized change to investigate and bring through the process
An approved change, because developers may approve their own work
An emergency change, because it was made outside working hours
why: Changes need approval by authorized personnel before deployment. A ticket after the fact does not make a change authorized, self-approval defeats separation of duties, and a true emergency uses a defined expedited path.

q: A change request has an approved schedule and test results but no rollback plan, and the maintenance window is tomorrow night. What should the change board do?
opts: Approve it because the test results look good and the schedule is set
Approve it and ask operations to improvise a rollback if needed
Hold approval until a rollback plan and success criteria exist
Cancel all future changes until a rollback policy is written
why: A rollback plan is part of deploying safely. Good tests do not replace it, improvising during failure is risky, and canceling all changes is out of proportion.

q: A team has only ever tested changes directly in production because the test environment is "out of date". What is the best improvement?
opts: Continue testing directly in production but only do it after working hours
Keep a production-like test environment and promote changes through it
Remove the test environment altogether to avoid any further confusion
Test only those changes that the product vendor flags as being risky
why: Changes are validated in an environment like production before deployment. Testing in production after hours still risks the live service, removing the test environment worsens the problem, and vendor flags alone are not a test strategy.

q: Configuration monitoring reports several changes on a server with no matching approved change records. What is the best response?
opts: Ignore them because monitoring tools often produce so many false alerts
Approve them all in one bulk request so that the change records match
Treat them as possible unauthorized changes and investigate them first
Disable the monitoring rule that produced the alerts to cut the noise
why: Changes without matching records are both a compliance gap and a possible security event, so they are investigated and then reversed or processed through change control. Ignoring, bulk-approving or disabling the rule hides the problem.

q: An exploit is being used against a public service late on Saturday, and the fix cannot wait for the weekly change board. What should happen?
opts: Wait until the regular change board meets again on Monday morning
Apply the fix without keeping any record, to avoid extra paperwork
Let the first available engineer decide alone and keep no record of it at all
Use the emergency path with designated approval, then review it later
why: Emergency procedures give a faster approval route with accountability and a later review. Waiting leaves the exploit open, and making unrecorded changes or leaving it to anyone defeats control.

q: A monitoring plan checks network devices and servers but says nothing about facility access, staff access reviews or unapproved changes. What is the best assessment?
opts: It omits physical assets, personnel and change control
It is complete, because only logical assets can be monitored
It is too broad, because monitoring should cover one device type only
It is correct, because personnel are monitored only by the HR department
why: Ongoing monitoring covers physical and logical assets, personnel and change control. The statement that only logical assets can be monitored is false, and personnel monitoring is part of the security program, not left to HR alone.

q: The contingency plan for a system was last exercised three years ago, and since then the system moved to a new data center. What is the best step?
opts: Leave the plan alone, since it passed the original test years ago
Exercise the plan in the new environment, record results and update it
Archive the plan and rely on the new hosting provider's own plan instead
Rewrite the plan to be shorter and simpler without ever testing it
why: Significant changes require the plan to be exercised again so gaps are found. A past passing result, handing over the responsibility or shortening the plan without testing leaves the assumption unverified.

q: A new state law adds a requirement for annual encryption verification for systems like yours. What is the best response?
opts: Wait for the next scheduled audit before looking at the new law and its scope
Update the mapping and monitoring strategy, reassess controls, inform stakeholders
Assume existing controls already comply and make no changes to documents or testing
Ask the vendor to update its marketing materials about encryption in its products
why: Changes in legal requirements feed back into the monitoring strategy and mapping, with reassessment of affected controls and communication to stakeholders. Waiting, assuming compliance or changing marketing leaves the obligation unmet.

q: A hosting provider announces new subprocessors that will handle the organization's data. Which action best supports ongoing compliance?
opts: Accept the change because suppliers are entitled to change without notice at all
Ask the provider to withdraw its notice so that the records stay unchanged
Record the change only in the provider's own internal documents and portals
Review it against requirements and update the contract, SLA and risk records
why: Supplier changes can alter risk and obligations, so the organization reviews them and updates its contracts, SLAs and risk records. Accepting silently or leaving the record with the provider loses oversight.

q: A merchant asks which recurring technical tests PCI DSS expects for its external systems. Which pair is closest to the requirement?
opts: Quarterly external scans by an approved vendor, annual penetration testing
Vulnerability scans every five years and no penetration testing at any time
Penetration testing every month and no vulnerability scans of any kind at all
Only a yearly review of written policies with no technical testing of any kind
why: PCI DSS expects quarterly external scans by an approved scanning vendor and penetration testing at least every 12 months and after significant change. The other options set intervals or omit tests that the standard requires.

q: During an audit of access control, the auditor interviews only the IT director. What is the best improvement?
opts: Interview several more directors and rely on their summaries of daily practice
Replace all interviews with a review of the written policy and nothing else
Ask the IT director to answer on behalf of the whole team and sign it off
Also interview the administrators who operate the control and corroborate
why: Interviews are most useful with the people who operate the control, and the answers are corroborated with documents and tests. Directors' summaries, policy review alone and proxy answers show intent, not practice.

q: A server is shut down for retirement, but its interconnection to a partner and several service accounts remain active. What was missed?
opts: Raising the impact level of the retired system before it is switched off
Writing a brand new system security plan and privacy plan for the retired system
Disconnecting interconnections and revoking access when removing the system
Authorizing the retired system for ongoing operation by the authorizing official
why: Removal from operation includes disconnecting interconnections, revoking access and updating inventories. Raising the level, writing a new plan or reauthorizing do not belong to retirement.

q: Data from a system scheduled for retirement is subject to a legal hold. What should the decommissioning plan do?
opts: Sanitize the media on schedule because the retirement date was set
Move the data to a personal laptop for convenience
Delete the data after copying only the summary report
Preserve the data in an approved archive while the hold applies
why: Legal holds override normal disposal. The plan archives the data and records the decision. Scheduled sanitization or deleting the data destroys material that must be kept.

q: Who should review the requirements for decommissioning a payroll system before it is shut down?
opts: The system owner, information owner, mission owner, AO and dependent system owners
Only the help desk manager, because it receives all the questions about the payroll system
Only the vendor, because it supplied the payroll software and knows how it works
Only the independent security assessor, who reviewed the system in the last assessment cycle
why: Retirement affects data retention, dependent systems and approvals, so the accountable stakeholders review the requirements together. A single group such as the help desk, vendor or assessor cannot cover them.

q: Which three belong in a change request record? (Choose three.)
opts: The personal opinions of staff about the change
The approvals by authorized personnel
The authorization termination date of the system
The rollback plan and success criteria
The impact analysis on risk, operations and compliance
why: A change record shows the impact analysis, rollback and success criteria and approvals. The termination date and personal opinions do not describe the change.

q: Which two are covered by ongoing monitoring of a system and its assets? (Choose two.)
opts: Only the marketing performance of the product
Changes made compared with changes approved
Only the color and layout of the user interface
Only the vendor's sales figures
Physical access to facilities that house the system
why: Monitoring covers physical and logical assets, personnel and change control. Interface layout, marketing performance and vendor sales are not control-related.

q: Which three should be retained and shared with stakeholders after decommissioning? (Choose three.)
opts: The decommissioning plan and checklist
Active administrator passwords for the retired system
The decommissioned system's live network access
The authorization termination notice
Certificates showing media sanitization or destruction
why: Records of the retirement, data disposition and termination are retained as evidence. Active credentials and live access should have been revoked, not kept.

q: Which two statements about contingency plan exercises are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A tabletop exercise walks through a scenario in discussion
A single successful test is valid regardless of later changes
Results are recorded and used to update the plan and training
Exercises are unnecessary when a plan is stored securely
why: Exercises range from discussion to full failover, and results drive updates. A past test does not cover later changes, and storing a plan securely does not show it works.

q: An emergency change may skip documentation permanently because speed matters most.
opts: True
False
why: The emergency path speeds up approval, but the change is still recorded and reviewed afterward, and permanent fixes go through the regular process.

q: A change may be deployed directly to production without testing as long as a rollback plan exists.
opts: True
False
why: A rollback plan limits damage but does not replace testing in an environment that resembles production.

q: Training records for incident response and contingency training should be retained as evidence.
opts: True
False
why: Completion records show that people were trained at the required times and are requested during audits.

q: Revisions to an approved baseline are made through change control and recorded.
opts: True
False
why: Baseline changes are approved and versioned so that comparison and monitoring use the correct reference.

q: Documentation of a decommissioned system is destroyed immediately because the system no longer exists.
opts: True
False
why: Records are retained for the required period and shared with stakeholders as evidence of proper disposal and for legal and audit needs.
